topic: European Trading Companies & Struggle for Supremacy

items.title: The Advent of Europeans & Order of Arrival
items.body:
## Why Europeans sought a sea route

- The **Age of Discoveries (15th–17th c.)** was driven by the search for **spices** (pepper, cinnamon, cloves) and a wish to **bypass Ottoman-controlled overland routes** and their heavy tolls.
- Advances in **navigation and shipbuilding**, national rivalries, and the urge to spread Christianity fuelled the voyages.

## Sequence of arrival (exam favourite)

**Portuguese → Dutch → English → Danish → French**

| Power | First factory | Year | Left India |
|---|---|---|---|
| Portuguese | Cochin | 1503 | 1961 |
| Dutch | Masulipatnam | 1605 | 1825 (ceded) |
| English | Surat | 1612–13 | 1947 |
| Danish | Tranquebar | 1620 | 1845 (sold) |
| French | Surat/Pondicherry | 1668/1674 | 1954 |

- Note the trap: the **English (1600) and Dutch (1602) companies** were founded before the **French company (1664)**, even though the French *reached* prominence later.
keyPoints: Order of arrival: Portuguese → Dutch → English → Danish → French.
Motive: direct spice trade + bypassing Ottoman overland routes; the 'Age of Discoveries'.
Portuguese were the first to come (1498) and the last to leave (Goa, 1961).
Dutch first factory = Masulipatnam (1605); English first factory = Surat (1612–13).
English EIC chartered 1600, Dutch VOC 1602, French company 1664.
items.mnemonic: Arrival order 'Please Do Eat Delicious Food' = Portuguese, Dutch, English, Danish, French.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Modern History: The Advent of Europeans

items.title: The Portuguese: Da Gama to the Blue Water Policy
items.body:
## Pioneers of the sea route

- **Bartholomeu Diaz** rounded the **Cape of Good Hope (1487)**; **Vasco da Gama** reached **Calicut in 1498**, received by the **Zamorin**.
- First Portuguese fort at **Cochin (1503)**; second at **Cannanore (1505)**.

## Key governors

- **Francisco Almeida** (first viceroy) — launched the **Blue Water (Cartaz) Policy** to master the Indian Ocean; won the **Battle of Diu (1509)** against the Egyptians, Arabs and Zamorin.
- **Alfonso de Albuquerque** — the **real founder of Portuguese power in the East**; **captured Goa from the Sultan of Bijapur (1510)**, abolished sati, encouraged Portuguese–Indian marriages.
- **Nino da Cunha** — shifted the capital from **Cochin to Goa (1530)**.

## Decline

- Lost their Malabar forts to the **Dutch by 1663**; religious intolerance (Jesuits) and piracy antagonised Mughals.
- **Goa, Daman and Diu** were the **last European possessions, liberated by India in 1961**.
keyPoints: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 (Zamorin); first fort at Cochin, 1503.
Almeida began the Blue Water Policy; Battle of Diu (1509) secured naval supremacy.
Albuquerque captured Goa (1510) and is the real founder of Portuguese power in the East.
Goa became the Portuguese capital in 1530 (Nino da Cunha).
Goa, Daman and Diu were liberated in 1961 — Portuguese were last to leave.
items.mnemonic: Portuguese governors A-A-N: Almeida (Blue Water) → Albuquerque (Goa) → Nino da Cunha (capital to Goa).
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Modern History: Portuguese

items.title: Dutch, English, Danish & French Companies
items.body:
## Dutch

- First factory at **Masulipatnam (1605)**; built **Fort Geldria at Pulicat**, the **headquarters of Dutch Coromandel**.
- Pursued a **redistributive Asian trade** (indigo, textiles, saltpetre, opium); prioritised the **East Indies (Indonesia)** and were pushed out by the British (e.g. Battle of Colachel, 1741).

## English

- **EIC chartered by Elizabeth I (1600)**; first factory at **Surat (1612–13)** after Hawkins/Sir Thomas Roe (farman from Jahangir, 1615).
- **Madras (Fort St. George, 1639)**; **Bombay** came as **Catherine of Braganza's dowry (1661)**, transferred to the EIC in **1668**.

## Danish

- Company **1616**; factory at **Tranquebar (1620)**; later **Serampore**; **sold to the British in 1845**. Remembered for **missionary work**.

## French

- Company reorganised by **Colbert (1664)**; **Francois Martin founded Pondicherry (1674)**.
- **Dupleix** (Governor-General from 1741) began **interfering in Indian succession disputes** and raised **mixed Indian–French regiments**.
keyPoints: Dutch: first factory Masulipatnam (1605); Fort Geldria at Pulicat = Coromandel HQ.
English EIC chartered 1600; Surat (1612–13), Madras/Fort St. George (1639), Bombay (dowry 1661, EIC 1668).
Sir Thomas Roe secured a trade farman from Jahangir in 1615.
Danish company 1616; Tranquebar (1620); sold to British in 1845.
French: Pondicherry founded by Francois Martin (1674); Dupleix pioneered political intervention.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Modern History: The Advent of Europeans; British East India Company

items.title: European Factories on the Andhra (Coromandel) Coast
items.body:
## Why the Andhra coast mattered

The **Coromandel coast** of Andhra was famed for **painted/printed cotton textiles** and lay on the sea lanes between Bengal and the south, so every company sought footholds here.

| Factory (modern name) | First / chief European power | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Masulipatnam** (Machilipatnam) | **Dutch (1605, first factory)**; English factory 1611 | Chief port of Golconda |
| **Nizampatnam** (Pettapoli) | **English** (early factory) | Southern Krishna delta |
| **Pulicat** | **Dutch** — Fort Geldria | HQ of Dutch Coromandel |
| **Bheemunipatnam** (Bimlipatam) | **Dutch** | Near Visakhapatnam |
| **Yanam** (Yanaon) | **French** | Near the Godavari mouth |

## Yanam's later story

- Retained by France under the **Treaty of Paris (1763)**; stayed French after 1947 and **merged with India in 1954**, now part of the **Union Territory of Puducherry**.
keyPoints: Masulipatnam: Dutch first factory (1605), English factory (1611); chief Golconda port.
Pulicat: Dutch Fort Geldria — headquarters of Dutch Coromandel.
Nizampatnam (Pettapoli) hosted an early English factory; Bheemunipatnam was a Dutch settlement.
Yanam was a French enclave near the Godavari, merged with India in 1954 (now Puducherry UT).
The Andhra coast was prized for its painted cotton textiles.
items.mnemonic: AP coast: Masulipatnam & Pulicat = Dutch, Nizampatnam = English, Yanam = French.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Modern History: The Advent of Europeans; standard references

items.title: The Carnatic Wars & the Northern Circars (1746–63)
items.body:
## Three Anglo-French wars in the south

| War | Years | Key event | Ended by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **First** | 1746–48 | French capture Madras; San Thome | **Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle** (Madras restored) |
| **Second** | 1749–54 | Succession disputes; **Clive takes Arcot (1751)**; Chanda Sahib executed | **Treaty of Pondicherry**; Dupleix recalled |
| **Third** | 1756–63 | **Battle of Wandiwash (1760)** — Eyre Coote beats Lally; Pondicherry falls (1761) | **Treaty of Paris (1763)** |

- The wars showed the **superiority of European-trained armies** and the tactic of **backing rival Indian claimants**; the English emerged the **paramount European power**.

## Northern Circars

- The five coastal Andhra tracts — **Srikakulam (Chicacole), Rajahmundry, Eluru, Kondapalli and Guntur**.
- **Bussy** first won them as a **grant from the Nizam**; during the Third Carnatic War the **Nizam transferred Masulipatnam and the Circars to the British**, who consolidated them through a **Mughal farman (1765)** and a treaty with the Nizam. The **Guntur Circar** passed fully to the British in **1788**.
keyPoints: First Carnatic War (1746–48) ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle; Madras restored.
Second Carnatic War (1749–54): Clive's Arcot exploit; Treaty of Pondicherry; Dupleix recalled.
Third Carnatic War: Battle of Wandiwash (1760, Eyre Coote v. Lally); Treaty of Paris (1763).
Northern Circars = Srikakulam, Rajahmundry, Eluru, Kondapalli, Guntur.
Bussy got the Circars from the Nizam; transferred to the British, confirmed by 1765 farman; Guntur in 1788.
items.mnemonic: Carnatic War enders 'ACP': Aix-la-Chapelle → (Treaty of) Pondicherry → Paris.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Modern History: Carnatic Wars; standard references

items.title: Plassey, Buxar & the Turn to Territorial Power
items.body:
## Battle of Plassey (1757)

- **Robert Clive** defeated **Siraj-ud-Daulah**, last independent Nawab of Bengal, through the **treachery of Mir Jafar**, who was then made puppet Nawab.
- Triggers: misuse of trade privileges, fortification of Calcutta, the **Black Hole** episode, and the capture of **Fort William**.
- Plassey gave the Company **military supremacy in Bengal** and huge wealth (zamindari of 24 Parganas).

## Battle of Buxar (1764)

- **Hector Munro** defeated the combined forces of **Mir Qasim (Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daulah (Awadh) and Shah Alam II (Mughal emperor)**.
- More decisive than Plassey — the Company defeated a **Mughal-led coalition**, becoming the real power in northern India.

## Treaty of Allahabad & Diwani (1765)

- Clive signed treaties granting the Company the **Diwani (revenue administration) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa** from Shah Alam II.
- This marked the **transition from a mercantile company to a territorial ruler**; Awadh was left as a **buffer state**.
keyPoints: Plassey (1757): Clive beat Siraj-ud-Daulah via Mir Jafar's betrayal; British supremacy in Bengal.
Buxar (1764): Munro beat Mir Qasim + Shuja-ud-Daulah + Shah Alam II — a Mughal-led coalition.
Buxar was more decisive than Plassey for British political mastery of the east.
Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
The Company thus turned from trader to territorial ruler; Awadh kept as a buffer state.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Modern History: Expansion of EIC — Plassey & Buxar

items.title: Charter Acts, Early Factories, Trade Goods & Missions (PYQ set)
items.body:
## English factories & Anglo-Dutch clashes

- Earliest EIC factories: **Surat (1613)** after the **Battle of Swally (Suvali, 1612)**, where the English defeated the Portuguese fleet and won Jahangir's goodwill; an inland factory at **Broach (Bharuch)** was among the first in the first quarter of the 17th century.
- **Amboyna Massacre (1623)** in the East Indies made the English quit the spice islands and concentrate on the Indian mainland.
- The Dutch were finally beaten by the English at the **Battle of Bedara (1759)** in Bengal, ending Dutch political ambitions in India.

## Staple exports from Bengal (mid-18th c.)

- The EIC exported **cotton textiles, raw silk, saltpetre and opium** from Bengal — saltpetre (for gunpowder) and Bengal silk/muslin were especially prized.

## Charter Acts & the end of Company trade

| Act | Key provision |
|---|---|
| **Charter Act 1813** | Ended the EIC's **trade monopoly except tea and trade with China**; asserted Crown sovereignty over Company territories; ₹1 lakh for education |
| **Charter Act 1833** | Ended **all** EIC trade; made it a purely administrative body; created the **Governor-General of India** (Bentinck first) |
| **Charter Act 1853** | Separated legislative & executive functions; open competition for the Civil Service |

- Company rule finally ended with the **Government of India Act 1858** and **Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 Nov 1858)**, which disclaimed further annexation and placed India under the Crown.

## Missionaries following the traders

- **St Francis Xavier** (Jesuit co-founder) evangelised the Portuguese Estado da India; his body lies at the **Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa** (he died on Shangchuan Island, China, 1552).
- First Protestant mission = **Danish-Halle Mission, Tranquebar (1706, Ziegenbalg)**; the **Serampore Trio (Carey, Marshman, Ward)** worked from the Danish enclave near Calcutta.
keyPoints: Surat factory (1613) followed the Battle of Swally (1612) vs the Portuguese; Broach was an early inland factory.
Amboyna Massacre (1623) pushed the English from the spice islands to mainland India; Dutch beaten at Bedara (1759).
Bengal staple exports (mid-18th c.): cotton textiles, raw silk, saltpetre and opium.
Charter Act 1813 ended EIC monopoly except tea & China trade; 1833 ended all trade + created GG of India; 1853 opened Civil Service.
Company rule ended by GoI Act 1858 + Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 Nov 1858).
St Francis Xavier (Jesuit) is entombed at Bom Jesus Basilica, Old Goa; died on Shangchuan I., China (1552).
items.mnemonic: Charter Acts end trade in steps: 1813 (except tea/China) → 1833 (all trade ends, GG of India) → 1853 (civil-service exam).
items.source: Standard references — Charter Acts 1813/1833/1853; Battle of Swally; Amboyna; St Francis Xavier
